title: Cover the Light, and the Glasses Stop Recording
hook: Meta's AI glasses will no longer record when the little privacy LED is blocked — closing the loophole that let a wearer film you with no visible sign at all.
key_points: Ars Technica reported on August 28, 2026 that Meta limited nonconsensual recording on its AI glasses.
The fix: the glasses stop recording when a user covers up the safety light that signals capture.
That LED is the only cue bystanders get — tape over it and recording looked like ordinary glasses.
Ars notes privacy risks remain; a hardware indicator is a norm, not an enforcement mechanism.
Practical habit: in public, assume any camera-glasses wearer may be recording you.
content_html: Meta's AI glasses have a small LED that lights up while they're recording. It's the entire consent mechanism: with a phone you can see someone raise it, but with glasses the light is the only tell. On August 28, 2026, Ars Technica reported that Meta closed the obvious hole — cover the light with tape or a finger and the glasses now stop recording rather than filming invisibly.
extra_html:
It's a real improvement and a narrow one. Ars's framing is that the glasses got "slightly less creepy" while privacy risks remain, which is about right: an indicator light asks a stranger to notice a small LED on someone's face across a room, and the fix only addresses deliberately blocking it.

The transferable lesson is about where privacy protections actually live. A social norm ("you can tell when you're on camera") only holds while the hardware enforces it, and hardware can be worked around. The practical habit for everyday life is the unglamorous one: in public, assume anyone wearing camera glasses might be recording, the same way you'd assume a security camera is on.

related.title: Apps That Spot Camera Glasses — Imperfectly
related.hook: As Meta's AI glasses get more capable, a wave of free apps promises to tell you when someone nearby is wearing a pair. Ars found they don't reliably work.

related.title: Your Data & Privacy
related.hook: When you type into a free AI tool, you might be the product. What you share can be stored, reviewed by humans, and used to train future models — so share like it's not private.

related.title: Facial Recognition
related.hook: The same AI that unlocks your phone can pick your face out of a crowd. It's convenient at your fingertips and unsettling at a city's scale — and it makes mistakes, unevenly.

flashcards.prompt: What is the privacy LED on camera glasses for?
flashcards.back_html: It's the only signal bystanders get that they're being recorded — a visible cue standing in for the obvious gesture of raising a phone.

flashcards.prompt: What loophole did Meta's change close?

choices.text: Covering the indicator light let someone record with no visible sign
The glasses uploaded video without Wi-Fi
Anyone could view another wearer's recordings
The glasses recorded audio even when powered off

flashcards.explanation_html: Tape over the LED and recording looked identical to just wearing glasses. Now the glasses refuse to record when the light is blocked.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a privacy indicator a weak protection on its own?
flashcards.back_html: It depends on bystanders noticing a small light and on the wearer not defeating it. Ars notes real privacy risks remain even after the fix.
